\chapter{Hecho, Dicho, Visto, Puesto}
\label{ch:irregular-participles}
\hlchaptermodality{114}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the four irregular participles and say why those four.}

Complete ES-C49-participios-irregulares: give the four forms, name the English noun that is hecho, and say why these four break the rule.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hecho · dicho · visto · puesto]{hecho, dicho, visto, puesto}

\label{lesson:ES-C49-participios-irregulares}



\begin{quote}
By the rule, the participle of \emph{hacer} should be \emph{hacido}. Say it. Now be told that nobody has ever said it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four, and you could have guessed which}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{participle} & \textbf{in use} \\
\midrule
\emph{hacer} & \textbf{hecho} & \emph{he hecho} — I have done \\
\emph{decir} & \textbf{dicho} & \emph{he dicho} — I have said \\
\emph{ver} & \textbf{visto} & \emph{he visto} — I have seen \\
\emph{poner} & \textbf{puesto} & \emph{he puesto} — I have put \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Look at that list of verbs before you look at the forms. \emph{Do}, \emph{say}, \emph{see}, \emph{put} — four of the commonest verbs in any language, and the same four that have been irregular in every tense you have met. The verbs that break rules are not a random selection: \textbf{they are always the ones said most often}, because frequent words are the only ones used enough to survive being irregular.

You already know this in English. \emph{Go/went}, \emph{see/saw}, \emph{do/did}, \emph{put/put} — and nobody struggles with them, because you meet them a hundred times a day. The same will happen here.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
These four are not broken. They are \textbf{older than the rule}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hecho} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{factum} — the thing done. English \textbf{fact} is that same word: a fact is literally \emph{a thing that has been done}.
  \item \emph{dicho} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{dictum} — the thing said. English keeps \emph{dictum} whole, and \emph{dictation}, \emph{verdict} (\textquotedblleft{}a true saying\textquotedblright{}), \emph{contradict}.
  \item \emph{visto} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{vīsum} — the thing seen. English \textbf{vision}, \textbf{visible}.
  \item \emph{puesto} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{positum} — the thing placed. English \textbf{position}, \textbf{deposit}, \textbf{compose}.
\end{itemize}

Latin already had participles for these verbs, and Spanish inherited them intact instead of rebuilding them from the stem. The regular \emph{-ado} / \emph{-ido} forms are the newer machinery; these four are what was there before it.

So an irregular participle is not a form that went wrong. It is a form that was never replaced.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hecho, dicho, visto, puesto\textquotedblright{}
  \item each with English beside it — \textquotedblleft{}hecho / fact\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}dicho / dictum\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}visto / vision\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}puesto / position\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The four? (\emph{\textbf{Hecho, dicho, visto, puesto}}.) Are they broken forms? (\textbf{No} — they are \textbf{older than the rule}, inherited whole from Latin.) Next: all of it together.
